claims.text: Vanadium, titanium, zirconium, hafnium, and chromium are low-activation refractory elements suitable for formulating the proposed HEA.
An HEA made exclusively from these low-activation refractory elements will maintain high-temperature mechanical performance under fusion plasma-facing conditions.
The proposed HEA will maintain irradiation resistance under fusion plasma-facing conditions.
The proposed HEA will exhibit reduced long-term radioactivity under fusion plasma-facing conditions.
The proposed material is an as-cast and appropriately heat-treated refractory HEA containing low-activation elements in near-equimolar proportions.
Temperatures above 1000°C are representative of high-temperature fusion plasma-facing conditions for the proposed test.
Multielement alloying produces solid-solution strengthening in the proposed HEA.
Multielement alloying produces nanoscale microstructural features that stabilize the alloy at high temperatures.
The selected elements do not produce significant quantities of long-lived radioactive isotopes upon neutron exposure.
The high-entropy effect stabilizes the alloy microstructure during high-temperature neutron irradiation.
High-entropy microstructural stabilization resists radiation-induced damage and thereby preserves mechanical properties.
The proposed HEA will sustain high-temperature mechanical integrity under the specified test conditions.
The proposed HEA will exhibit minimal radiation-induced degradation.
The proposed HEA will have lower residual radioactivity than conventional plasma-facing materials under similar reactor conditions.
Tungsten and ferritic-martensitic steels can suffer from comparatively high activation or degradation under extreme fusion conditions.
Temperatures or irradiation fluxes beyond the design limits may cause the alloy to fail.
Long-term exposure may produce unforeseen phase instabilities that cause the alloy to fail.
Experimental data for the proposed composition under reactor-level conditions are insufficient to establish its long-term irradiation response and low-activation behavior.
